blurb: What happens between your phone and the internet on mobile data: cells, SIMs, spectrum, handovers, and what 5G really changed.

lessons.title: From your phone to the internet

cards.title: The journey of one tap

steps.p: Your phone talks by radio to a nearby base station — the antennas on a mast or rooftop. Each one covers an area called a cell.
The base station passes your data over fibre or a point-to-point microwave link, called backhaul, into the operator's private network.
The operator's core checks who you are, gives your phone an internet address, tracks which cell you're in, and hands traffic out to the wider internet.

cards.aside: Only the first few hundred metres or kilometres are wireless. Almost everything after the mast travels by cable.

cards.q: Why is mobile coverage called a "cellular" network?
options: The area is split into many small zones, each served by its own base station
It was invented by biologists studying cells
Data is stored in memory cells on the tower
cards.why: It's a patchwork of cells. Splitting an area into many small zones lets the same radio frequencies be reused a few cells away, so millions of phones can share limited spectrum.

cards.statement: When you call someone standing right next to you, your two phones talk to each other directly.
cards.why: False. Both phones connect to the network separately. The call travels up to a base station, through the operator's core, and back down, even if you're a metre apart.

cards.q: What is "backhaul" in a mobile network?
options: The radio link between your phone and the mast
The link carrying traffic from base stations back into the operator's network
cards.why: The mast's link home. Backhaul, usually fibre or microwave, connects each base station to the core. A strong signal can still feel slow if that link is overloaded.

cards.title: A single cell can cover a few hundred metres in a city or tens of kilometres in open countryside.
cards.detail: Cities use many small cells because more cells means more capacity for dense crowds. Rural areas use big cells because there are fewer people to serve per mast.

cards.why: True. Each generation is a new set of standards. 1G was analogue voice, 2G went digital and added texts, 3G brought usable mobile internet, and 4G made data the main event.

cards.title: How millions of phones share the air

steps.p: Governments sell operators exclusive rights to bands of radio frequencies. Unlike Wi-Fi's free bands, nobody else may transmit on them, which keeps interference low.
The base station divides its band into tiny slices of frequency and time, and schedules which phone gets which slice, thousands of times a second.
Your phone constantly measures nearby cells. As you move, the network switches you to a stronger one mid-download, usually without you noticing.

cards.aside: Your data share drops when the cell is busy: everyone connected splits the same airtime.

cards.q: What does a SIM card mainly do?
options: Proves to the network which subscriber you are
cards.why: It's your identity. The SIM stores a subscriber number and a secret key. The network sends a random challenge, the SIM answers using the key, and the key itself never travels over the air.

cards.statement: An eSIM still holds a secret key; it's just a chip built into the phone that downloads operator profiles.
cards.why: True. An eSIM does the same identity job as a plastic SIM. The difference is that operator profiles are installed over the internet instead of by swapping a card.

cards.q: Why do operators value low frequencies, below about 1 GHz?
options: They carry far more data per second
They travel further and get through walls better
They use less battery on the mast
cards.why: Range and reach. Lower frequencies spread further and pass through buildings more easily, so they give wide, reliable coverage. The trade-off is less bandwidth and lower top speeds.

cards.title: A 2021 US auction of mid-band 5G spectrum raised more than $80 billion.
cards.detail: The C-band frequencies hit a sweet spot of decent range and high capacity. Operators paid that much because spectrum is the scarce raw material of a mobile network.

cards.statement: When you roam abroad, the foreign network checks your identity with your home operator.
cards.why: True. The visited network contacts your home operator, which holds your secret key data, to confirm you're a real subscriber. That's also how your home operator can bill you.

cards.title: What 5G actually changed

steps.p: 5G adds wide new bands, especially mid-band around 3.5 GHz, and very high millimetre-wave bands, giving far more room for data.
Masts use arrays of many small antennas to steer focused beams at individual phones, called beamforming, instead of spraying signal everywhere.
Shorter time slots and redesigned networks cut latency — the round-trip delay — which matters for gaming, video calls and machines talking to machines.

cards.aside: Most early 5G ran on top of a 4G core, called non-standalone 5G. Fully standalone 5G cores came later.

cards.q: Millimetre-wave 5G can be extremely fast. What's its big weakness?
options: Very short range, easily blocked by walls, trees, even a hand
cards.why: Short and fragile range. Frequencies above about 24 GHz carry huge capacity but fade quickly and struggle to pass obstacles. They suit stadiums and busy streets, not wide coverage.

cards.q: Roughly how much mobile data does an hour of HD video streaming use?
cards.why: About 1–3 GB. It depends on the app and resolution. Video is by far the biggest user of mobile data, which is why streaming apps offer a data-saver quality setting.

cards.statement: Seeing a 5G icon guarantees your connection is faster than 4G.
cards.why: False. The icon can show for slow low-band 5G or a weak signal, and speed also depends on how busy the cell and its backhaul are. A good 4G link can beat poor 5G.

cards.title: The first text message, sent in December 1992, said simply "Merry Christmas".
cards.detail: It was typed on a computer and sent to a phone on the UK's Vodafone network. Texts were squeezed into spare capacity on 2G's signalling channels, hence their short length.

cards.statement: Beamforming means a mast aims focused signal toward individual phones.
cards.why: True. By timing signals across many antenna elements, the mast makes waves add up in one direction and cancel elsewhere. Phones get stronger signal and nearby users interfere less.

cards.title: Why mobile data misbehaves

steps.p: At a concert or stadium, thousands of phones split the same airtime. Full bars, yet nothing loads: the cell is congested, not out of range.
Far from a mast, your phone turns its transmitter up and retries more often, so a poor signal drains the battery faster.
At the edge of a cell, the signal is noisier, so the phone uses slower, more robust ways of encoding data to keep the link alive.

cards.aside: Indoors, walls and energy-saving glass can weaken signal a lot, which is why phones often switch to Wi-Fi calling.

cards.statement: The number of signal bars tells you how fast your mobile data will be.
cards.why: False. Bars show signal strength only. Speed also depends on how many people share the cell, the backhaul behind it, and the network's own capacity.

cards.q: Why can 5G radio waves not damage DNA the way X-rays can?
options: They are non-ionising: each photon has far too little energy to break chemical bonds
Phones filter out the harmful part
cards.why: Non-ionising radiation. Radio photons carry millions of times less energy than X-ray photons. Their only established effect is slight heating, and safety limits keep that well below harmful levels.

cards.title: A typical phone transmits at about a fifth of a watt at most — far less than a small light bulb.
cards.detail: And it usually uses much less. The network tells each phone to turn its power down when close to a mast, saving battery and reducing interference for others.

cards.q: Your plan runs out mid-month. Which change usually saves the most data?
options: Lowering video streaming quality and stopping autoplay
cards.why: Video is the big one. Streaming and autoplaying clips dwarf messaging and browsing. Bluetooth and brightness affect battery, not data, and closed apps rarely use much.

cards.title: Find your data-hungry apps
cards.body: Your phone tracks mobile data used by each app. A couple of video or social apps usually account for most of it, often through autoplay or background refresh.
cards.challenge: Open Settings → Mobile/Cellular, scroll to the app list, and switch off mobile data or autoplay for your top data user.
